newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban advance despite north rout.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban advance despite north rout.

text.p: The Taleban militia advanced further into opposition territory in northeast Afghanistan on Thursday despite its rout in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif, witnesses and Afghan source said.
The purist militia said it also fought off new opposition counter-attacks north of the capital Kabul, losing some territory but regaining it later.

Opposition factions said they took three towns north of Kabul in an apparent drive to isolate an advancing Taleban convoy that had reached Pul-i-Khumri town in Baghlan province on Wednesday after crossing the strategic Salang Pass.

A Taleban spokesmen, quoted by a Pakistan-based Afghan news service, confirmed that opposition forces commanded by renowned guerrilla commander Ahmad Shah Masood launched "a big attack" and captured some Taleban territory.
But he said Masood's forces were later forced to abandon the captured territory and leave many dead.

The Taleban forces were in firm control of the Pul-i-Khumri on the second day of their arrival in the town but there was fighting on the road to Mazar-i-Sharif, 160 km (100 miles) to the north, witnesses said.

The Taleban spokesman, quoted by the Afghan Islamic Press (AIP), said the militia convoy of tanks and other vehicles had entered adjoining Samangan province after destroying an opposition front line at Rabatak and then moved towards the provincial capital, Aibek, which has changed hands twice in the past week.
AIP quoted the spokesman as saying Taleban forces advancing from the northeast would soon enter Balkh province, of which Mazar-i-Sharif is the capital, and then head for Mazar-i-Sharif itself.
He said Taleban forces still controlled most of the area around the airport in Mazar-i-Sharif, from where the Taleban forces were driven out on Wednesday.
The Foreign Ministry in neighbouring Pakistan said it had information the purist Islamic militia was engaged in peace talks with its opponents in Mazar-i-Sharif.

AIP quoted sources in Masood's Jamiat-i-Islami faction as saying his forces attacked the Taleban frontline early on Thursday and later captured the towns of Golbahar, Jabal-os-Siraj and Charikar, all north of Kabul.
The Taleban faced fresh fighting also on another front, in Bamiyan, with a Shi'ite Moslem militia.

A Pakistan Foreign Ministry spokesman told reporters in Islamabad the Taleban were holding peace talks in Mazar-i-Sharif with their opponents, who drove the militia out on Thursday after an alliance struck a few days earlier collapsed.
The spokesman, quoting reports received in Islamabad, said "negotiations are currently under way in Afghanistan to remove differences among various groups".

Pakistan was the first country to recognise the Taleban government after the capture of Mazar-i-Sharif, the main opposition stronghold in the north previously held by the forces of northern opposition warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum.

The spokesman said Pakistan had information "there were some differences" that led to the latest fighting in Mazar between the Taleban and Uzbek General Abdul Malik, who had defected from Dostum and allied himself with the militia. "They are talking to each other now."
Also involved in the talks was the opposition Hezb-i-Wahdat faction of Shi'ite Moslems, who fought alongside Malik's forces to drive the Taleban out of Mazar-i-Sharif.
Dostum, now in Ankara, was quoted by Turkey's state-run Anatolian news agency as saying that he wanted to make peace General Malik and wanted the Turkish government to mediate between the two men.
Dostum, an ethnic Uzbek, fled to Turkey after his ouster. He has been in an Ankara hotel since May 24.
Turkey said on Monday that Dostum could stay in the country as long as he wanted. Turks and Uzbeks share ethnic and linguistic links.
